title: Address Validator: How Geocoders Resolve It
description: See how open geocoders resolve an address before you trust it, with the Address Validator — matched place, coordinates, confidence. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a mailing list's 'Main St, Springfield' resolves confidently to the wrong Springfield unless a human reads the matched place before the batch goes out.

faq: Is this postal certification?
No. It shows open-geocoder resolution for your judgement. Certified address verification (for bulk-mail discounts and the like) is a regulated service this free tool does not impersonate.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — you type the address being checked; your own location plays no part.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Geocoders and maps draw from different sources and dates. A name that differs across services is a data-vintage story, not necessarily an error.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
No — and this tool never asks for it.
What makes a match trustworthy?
Specificity: a full address resolving to an address-level point in the expected town. Centroid matches in the wrong county are the classic warning.
The geocoder found nothing.
Rebuild the address: number, street, town, state, postcode, country — in that completeness order. Most failures are missing rungs, not missing places.
Fifty addresses to check?
The Batch Geocoder takes lists to 50 and returns a table you can audit in a spreadsheet.
The match is a town centroid — usable?
For a county-level question, maybe; for a delivery, no. Precision grades the uses a match can serve.
Two geocoders disagree about my address.
Trust the one whose matched place reads like your input, and suspect your input's completeness first. Disagreement is information, delivered free.
Does validation fix the address?
It shows the resolution; corrections are yours to make in the source data. A validator that silently rewrites would hide the very errors you are hunting.
